title: History
blurb: The turning points of humanity, and Portugal's leap into the open ocean.

lessons.title: Turning points of humanity
lessons.summary: Five changes that made the modern world, in the order they happened.

cards.title: Human history as one day
cards.text:
Squeeze the roughly 300,000 years of Homo sapiens into a single day. For almost all of it, everyone lived as hunter-gatherers.

Farming only starts at about 23:02. Writing appears at 23:36. The printing press arrives less than three minutes before midnight, and everything since the steam engine fits in the last minute.

cards.title: Farming changed everything
cards.text:
Around 10,000 BCE, people in the Fertile Crescent (today's Iraq, Syria and Turkey) began planting wheat and barley and keeping animals.

Farming made food surpluses possible. Surpluses could be stored, traded and taxed, and they fed people who didn't farm: potters, priests, soldiers and kings. Villages grew into the first cities.

cards.title: Writing started as bookkeeping
cards.text:
The oldest writing we know comes from Sumer, in today's Iraq, around 3200 BCE. It wasn't poetry. It was accounts: who delivered how much barley, how many sheep, how much beer was paid as wages.

Scribes pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay with a reed. We call the script cuneiform, from the Latin for 'wedge'.

cards.title: The printing press
cards.text:
Around 1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type, oil-based ink and a press adapted from wine making. A book that took a scribe months could now be printed by the hundred.

Within 50 years millions of books were in circulation. Ideas spread faster than authorities could control them, feeding the Reformation and the scientific revolution.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s" d="M80 30L80 150"/><path class="s" d="M240 30L240 150"/><path class="s" d="M68 30L252 30"/><path class="s" d="M160 32L153 35.7L167 43L153 50.3L167 57.7L153 65L167 72.3L160 76"/><path class="s" d="M128 60L192 60"/><rect class="s bgf" x="110" y="78" width="100" height="16" rx="3"/><rect class="w" x="115" y="110" width="90" height="10" rx="0"/><rect class="s bgf" x="100" y="120" width="120" height="14" rx="3"/><path class="s" d="M56 150L264 150"/></g><text class="a" x="252" y="58" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">screw</text><text class="a" x="252" y="120" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">type &</text><text class="a" x="252" y="138" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">paper</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">Gutenberg, Mainz, ~1450</text></svg>

cards.title: The Industrial Revolution
cards.text:
From about 1760 in Britain, machines powered by water and then coal-fired steam engines took over spinning, weaving and mining. Work moved from homes and fields into factories, and people moved into fast-growing cities.

For the first time in history, output per person kept rising decade after decade. It also brought child labour, pollution and the start of large-scale CO₂ emissions.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s bgf" d="M30 150 V102 L70 80 V102 L110 80 V102 L150 80 V150 Z"/><rect class="s bgf" x="160" y="44" width="20" height="106" rx="0"/><path class="dash" d="M170 38 q-12 -8 2 -16 q14 -8 6 -18"/><path class="s" d="M18 150L302 150"/><circle class="s" cx="250" cy="112" r="32"/><path class="s" d="M250 80L250 144"/><path class="s" d="M218 112L282 112"/><path class="s" d="M227 89L273 135"/><path class="s" d="M273 89L227 135"/><circle class="s bgf" cx="250" cy="112" r="6"/></g><text class="" x="90" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">factories</text><text class="r" x="250" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">steam power</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">Britain, from ~1760</text></svg>

cards.title: Fire and tools
cards.text: Long before farming, humans controlled fire, cooked food and made ever better stone tools. Cooking made food easier to digest and may have helped our ancestors grow bigger brains.

cards.title: Out of Africa
cards.text: Modern humans evolved in Africa and spread across the world in waves, reaching Europe around 45,000 years ago, Australia perhaps 50,000–65,000 years ago and the Americas at least 15,000 years ago.

cards.title: Cities and states
cards.text: With farming came the first cities in Mesopotamia, such as Uruk and Ur, around 4000–3000 BCE: temples, kings, laws, taxes and soldiers.

cards.title: Money
cards.text: Before coins, people traded goods or used standard weights of silver and grain. The first coins appeared in Lydia (modern Turkey) around 600 BCE. China later invented paper money.

cards.title: The internet age
cards.text: The latest turning point: computers, the internet and smartphones connected most of humanity within a few decades and changed how we work, learn and communicate.

quiz.q: What was most early writing used for?
options: Keeping accounts of goods and payments
quiz.explain: The earliest Sumerian tablets are mostly records of grain, livestock and rations.

quiz.q: Why did farming lead to cities?
options: Food surpluses could feed people who didn't farm
Cities were needed to store tools
quiz.explain: Surplus food supported specialists, rulers and traders, which made towns and cities possible.

quiz.q: Where and when did Gutenberg's press appear?
quiz.explain: Gutenberg worked in Mainz around 1450. (Movable type existed earlier in China and Korea, but his press transformed Europe.)

quiz.q: Where did Homo sapiens first evolve?
quiz.explain: Modern humans spread out from Africa.

quiz.q: Where were the first coins minted?

lessons.title: Portugal and the Age of Discovery
lessons.summary: How a small kingdom at the edge of Europe opened the world's sea routes.

cards.title: Why Portugal turned to the sea
cards.text:
In the 1400s Portugal was small, poor and boxed in by Castile. The rich trade in spices and silk came overland from Asia and was controlled by Venice and Muslim middlemen.

The Atlantic was the one open door. Prince Henry 'the Navigator' sponsored expeditions down the African coast, step by step, hoping to reach gold, allies and eventually the spices of India by sea.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="a" d="M60 34 C34 62 30 96 58 124 C92 156 140 162 178 142 C222 118 262 90 300 62"/><circle class="fred" cx="60" cy="34" r="6"/><circle class="fred" cx="40" cy="80" r="5"/><circle class="fred" cx="178" cy="142" r="5"/><circle class="fred" cx="300" cy="62" r="6"/></g><text class="" x="74" y="34" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:17px">Lisbon</text><text class="" x="52" y="84" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">Cape Bojador 1434</text><text class="" x="178" y="166" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Cape of Good Hope 1488</text><text class="r" x="300" y="44" text-anchor="end" style="font-size:17px">India 1498</text><text class="a" x="170" y="114" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">sea route (schematic)</text></svg>

cards.title: The caravel
cards.text:
Square sails work beautifully with the wind behind you, but badly against it. The caravel's triangular 'lateen' sails let it sail much closer into the wind, and its shallow hull could explore coasts and rivers.

That mattered: coming home from West Africa meant fighting the prevailing winds. Explorers learned to swing far out into the Atlantic to catch better ones.

cards.title: Finding latitude from the stars
cards.text:
On open water there are no landmarks. In the northern hemisphere, the height of the Pole Star above the horizon roughly equals your latitude. Sailors measured it with a quadrant or astrolabe.

Further south the Pole Star disappears, so Portuguese navigators measured the Sun at noon instead and used printed tables to correct for the season.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s" d="M20 140L300 140"/><circle class="s bgf" cx="84" cy="114" r="6"/><path class="s" d="M84 120L84 132"/><path class="s" d="M84 132L78 140"/><path class="s" d="M84 132L90 140"/><path class="s" d="M84 125L96 121"/><path class="a" d="M96 118L240 46"/><path class="dash" d="M96 118L220 118"/><path class="r" d="M156 118 A60 60 0 0 0 150 91"/><path class="fred" d="M246.0 31.0 L248.9 38.0 L256.5 38.6 L250.7 43.5 L252.5 50.9 L246.0 47.0 L239.5 50.9 L241.3 43.5 L235.5 38.6 L243.1 38.0 Z"/></g><text class="r" x="166" y="108" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:16px">angle ≈ latitude</text><text class="" x="240" y="22" text-anchor="end" style="font-size:16px">Pole Star</text><text class="" x="160" y="166" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Lisbon: the Pole Star sits about 39° up</text></svg>

cards.title: The great voyages
cards.text:
Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488. Ten years later Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India, opening the sea route to the spice trade and making Lisbon one of Europe's richest ports.

In 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral, heading for India, swung so far west that he reached Brazil. And Fernão de Magalhães (Magellan), a Portuguese sailing for Spain, led the first voyage around the world, completed by Elcano in 1522.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="a" d="M20 92L300 92"/><circle class="fred" cx="40" cy="92" r="6"/><circle class="fred" cx="100" cy="92" r="6"/><circle class="fred" cx="160" cy="92" r="6"/><circle class="fred" cx="220" cy="92" r="6"/><circle class="fred" cx="280" cy="92" r="6"/></g><text class="r" x="40" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1419</text><text class="" x="40" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Madeira</text><text class="" x="40" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px"></text><text class="r" x="100" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1488</text><text class="" x="100" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Dias:</text><text class="" x="100" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Good Hope</text><text class="r" x="160" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1498</text><text class="" x="160" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">da Gama:</text><text class="" x="160" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">India</text><text class="r" x="220" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1500</text><text class="" x="220" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Cabral:</text><text class="" x="220" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Brazil</text><text class="r" x="280" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1522</text><text class="" x="280" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">round the</text><text class="" x="280" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">world</text><text class="" x="160" y="168" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:14px">not to scale</text></svg>

cards.title: Splitting the world: Tordesillas
cards.text:
In 1494 Portugal and Castile signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, drawing a line from pole to pole 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. New lands to the west would go to Castile, to the east to Portugal.

The tip of South America that bulged east of the line became Brazil, which is a big part of why around 210 million Brazilians speak Portuguese today.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><circle class="s bgf" cx="160" cy="98" r="64"/><ellipse class="dash" cx="160" cy="98" rx="32" ry="64"/><path class="dash" d="M96 98L224 98"/><path class="r" d="M136 26L136 172"/></g><text class="" x="62" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">Castile</text><text class="a" x="262" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">Portugal</text><text class="a" x="160" y="136" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">Brazil</text><text class="r" x="12" y="22" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:20px">1494</text><text class="r" x="308" y="22" text-anchor="end" style="font-size:13px">370 leagues W of Cape Verde</text></svg>

cards.title: Prince Henry's role
cards.text: Infante D. Henrique (1394–1460) didn't sail far himself, but he organised and funded voyages down the African coast from the Algarve, gathering pilots, mapmakers and shipbuilders.

cards.title: The spice trade

steps: Spices in India and the Moluccas

cards.text: Pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg were worth fortunes in Europe. The sea route to India let Portugal buy at the source, bypassing Venetian and Middle Eastern middlemen.

cards.title: The Portuguese in Asia
cards.text: Portugal built a network of trading posts and forts: Goa (1510), Malacca (1511), Hormuz and later Macau (1557). Portuguese traders were the first Europeans to reach Japan, in 1543.

cards.title: The dark side

items: Abolished in Portugal's empire in stages in the 1800s

cards.text: The voyages also opened the Atlantic slave trade. Over three and a half centuries, Portuguese and Brazilian ships carried more enslaved Africans across the Atlantic than any other nation's, a history now studied and acknowledged.

cards.title: Legacy of the discoveries
cards.text: The voyages connected continents, spread crops (maize, potatoes, tomatoes to Europe; sugar, coffee to the Americas), languages and diseases, and began globalisation, with both benefits and great suffering.

quiz.q: What could a caravel do better than a square-rigged ship?
options: Sail faster with the wind behind
quiz.explain: Its lateen sails let it work into the wind, essential for exploring and getting home.

quiz.q: Who first reached India by sea from Europe?
quiz.explain: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.

quiz.q: Why does Brazil speak Portuguese?
options: Cabral claimed it and it lay on Portugal's side of the Tordesillas line
quiz.explain: Cabral landed in 1500, and the land fell east of the 1494 treaty line.

quiz.q: Where was Portugal's main base in India?
Who were the first Europeans to reach Japan, in 1543?

lessons.title: Ancient Egypt
lessons.summary: Pyramids, pharaohs and the gift of the Nile.

cards.title: The gift of the Nile
cards.text: Egypt's civilisation grew along the Nile. Each year the river flooded and left fertile black silt, letting farmers grow wheat and barley in the middle of the desert.

cards.title: Three kingdoms
cards.text: Egyptian history spans about 3,000 years, usually divided into the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, separated by periods of disunity.

cards.title: The pyramids
cards.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE, with about 2.3 million stone blocks. It was the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.

cards.title: Who built them?

items.r: built by organised, paid labour teams

cards.text: Not slaves, as often claimed, but organised teams of paid workers and farmers working during the flood season, housed in villages nearby. Their tombs and bakeries have been excavated.

cards.title: Hieroglyphs

steps: Same text in Greek and Egyptian scripts

cards.text: Egyptians wrote with hieroglyphs: pictures standing for sounds and ideas. The Rosetta Stone, carrying the same text in three scripts, let Champollion decode them in 1822.

cards.title: Mummies
cards.text: Egyptians believed the body was needed in the afterlife. Embalmers removed organs, dried the body with natron salt for about 40 days and wrapped it in linen.

cards.title: Pharaohs and gods
cards.text: The pharaoh was seen as a living god and link between people and the divine. Egyptians worshipped many gods: Ra the sun, Osiris of the afterlife, Isis, Horus and Anubis.

cards.title: Tutankhamun
cards.text: A minor boy-king who died around 19, Tutankhamun became famous because his tomb was found almost intact by Howard Carter in 1922, full of treasures including the golden mask.

cards.title: Egyptian science
cards.text: Egyptians developed a 365-day calendar, practical geometry for re-measuring fields after floods, medicine recorded on papyrus and remarkable engineering.

cards.title: Cleopatra
cards.text: Cleopatra VII, the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic kingdom, was of Macedonian Greek descent. After her defeat with Mark Antony, Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE.

quiz.q: Why did Egyptian farming depend on the Nile?
options: Its yearly flood left fertile silt

quiz.q: What helped decode hieroglyphs?
Who built the pyramids?

lessons.title: Ancient Greece
lessons.summary: Democracy, philosophy and the Olympics.

cards.title: City-states
cards.text: Ancient Greece wasn't one country but hundreds of city-states (poleis) like Athens, Sparta, Corinth and Thebes, sharing a language and gods but often at war with each other.

cards.title: Athenian democracy
cards.text: From around 508 BCE, Athenian citizens voted directly on laws in the Assembly. But only free adult men counted as citizens: women, slaves and foreigners were excluded.

cards.title: Philosophy
cards.text: Greek thinkers asked how we should live and how the world works. Socrates questioned everything, Plato founded the Academy, Aristotle studied everything from logic to biology.

cards.title: The Persian Wars
cards.text: Persia's huge empire invaded Greece twice. The Greeks won at Marathon (490 BCE), held the pass at Thermopylae long enough, and won the naval battle of Salamis (480 BCE).

cards.title: The Olympics
cards.text: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia every four years from 776 BCE, in honour of Zeus. Wars paused for the games. The modern Olympics were revived in Athens in 1896.

cards.title: Alexander the Great
cards.text: Alexander of Macedon conquered an empire from Greece to Egypt and India before dying at 32 in 323 BCE. Greek language and culture spread across the region (the Hellenistic age).

cards.title: Greek science
cards.text: Euclid's geometry, Archimedes' physics, Hippocrates' medicine and Eratosthenes' measurement of Earth's circumference all came from the Greek world.

cards.title: Measuring the Earth
cards.text: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes compared the Sun's angle at noon in Syene and Alexandria. From a 7° difference and the distance between the cities, he estimated Earth's circumference remarkably well.

cards.title: Theatre
cards.text: Greeks invented tragedy and comedy as theatre forms. Huge open-air theatres like Epidaurus have such good acoustics that a whisper on stage can be heard in the back rows.

cards.title: Words we still use
cards.text: Many English and Portuguese words come from Greek: democracy, philosophy, theatre, telephone, biology, geography, mathematics.

quiz.q: Who could vote in Athenian democracy?
Who was Aristotle's famous student?
When were the modern Olympics revived?
quiz.explain: Pierre de Coubertin led the revival.

lessons.title: The Roman Empire
lessons.summary: From a small city to ruling the Mediterranean, including Lusitania.

cards.title: Kingdom, republic, empire
cards.text: By tradition Rome was founded in 753 BCE. It was ruled by kings, then became a republic governed by elected officials and the Senate, then an empire under Augustus from 27 BCE.

cards.title: The empire's size
cards.text: At its peak around 117 CE under Trajan, the empire stretched from Britain to Mesopotamia and from the Rhine to North Africa, with perhaps 50–70 million people.

cards.title: Lusitania
cards.text: Much of today's Portugal became the Roman province of Lusitania, with its capital at Emerita Augusta (Mérida). The Lusitanian leader Viriato resisted Rome fiercely until his murder in 139 BCE.

cards.title: Roman Portugal today
cards.text: You can still see Roman Portugal: the temple at Évora, the ruins of Conímbriga, the bridge at Chaves, and countless roads. Portuguese itself descends from Latin.

cards.title: Roads and aqueducts
cards.text: Romans built about 80,000 km of paved roads and aqueducts carrying water by gravity over long distances, using gentle slopes and arches.

cards.title: Roman concrete
cards.text: Romans used volcanic ash in concrete that has lasted 2,000 years, even in seawater. The Pantheon's dome in Rome, finished around 125 CE, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome.

cards.title: Roman law
cards.text: Roman law, later compiled under Emperor Justinian, is the basis of civil law systems across Europe and Latin America, including Portugal's.

cards.title: Latin's children
cards.text: Latin evolved into Portuguese, Spanish, Italian, French and Romanian. About 60% of English vocabulary also comes from Latin, directly or through French.

cards.title: The fall of the West
cards.text: The western empire weakened through civil wars, economic trouble and pressure from Germanic peoples. In 476 the last western emperor was deposed. The eastern (Byzantine) empire lasted until 1453.

cards.title: Christianity
cards.text: Christianity spread through the empire despite persecutions. Emperor Constantine legalised it in 313, and by 380 it became the official religion.

quiz.q: What was Roman Portugal largely called?
Which Lusitanian leader resisted Rome?
When did the western Roman Empire end?
quiz.explain: The last western emperor was deposed in 476.

lessons.title: The Middle Ages
lessons.summary: Castles, monasteries, knights and plague.

cards.title: A thousand years
cards.text: The Middle Ages run roughly from the fall of Rome (476) to the late 1400s. The name was coined later by Renaissance thinkers who saw it as a gap between antiquity and their own time.

cards.title: Feudalism
cards.text: Land was the main source of wealth. Kings granted land to lords in return for military service; peasants worked the land for lords in return for protection.

cards.title: The Church
cards.text: The Catholic Church was the most powerful institution in western Europe: it owned land, ran schools and hospitals, kept learning alive in monasteries and shaped daily life.

cards.title: Castles
cards.text: Castles were fortified homes and military bases. Portugal has hundreds, many built or rebuilt during the Reconquista: Guimarães, Almourol, Óbidos, Marvão.

cards.title: Crusades
cards.text: From 1096, Christian armies launched crusades to take Jerusalem and the Holy Land. Crusaders also helped Afonso Henriques conquer Lisbon in 1147 on their way east.

cards.title: The Black Death
cards.text: Plague swept Europe from 1347, carried by fleas on rats and spread between people. It killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population within a few years.

cards.title: After the plague
cards.text: With so many workers dead, survivors could demand higher wages and more freedom. Serfdom weakened in western Europe, and new ideas took root.

cards.title: Gothic cathedrals
cards.text: From the 1100s, pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses let builders raise tall, light cathedrals with huge stained-glass windows. The Batalha monastery is a Portuguese masterpiece.

cards.title: Universities
cards.text: Europe's first universities appeared in Bologna (1088), Paris and Oxford. Portugal's university was founded in Lisbon in 1290 and later moved permanently to Coimbra in 1537.

cards.title: The medieval world wasn't "dark"
cards.text: The Middle Ages brought windmills, eyeglasses, mechanical clocks, the compass in Europe, universities and great art. The idea of "dark ages" is now seen as too simple.

quiz.q: What killed perhaps a third of Europe in the 1300s?
Who helped Afonso Henriques take Lisbon in 1147?
Where did Portugal's university settle permanently in 1537?
quiz.explain: It moved between Lisbon and Coimbra before settling.

lessons.title: Al-Andalus
lessons.summary: Muslim Iberia and the Islamic golden age.

cards.title: 711: a new era in Iberia

events.l: most of Iberia under Muslim rule

cards.text: In 711, Muslim armies from North Africa crossed into Iberia and within a few years controlled most of the peninsula, including today's Portugal. They called it al-Andalus.

cards.title: Córdoba
cards.text: In the 10th century Córdoba was one of Europe's largest and most sophisticated cities, with paved streets, lighting, baths, libraries and the great mosque.

cards.title: Three faiths
cards.text: Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side in al-Andalus, with Christians and Jews as protected but taxed minorities. Coexistence was real but not equality, and it varied over time.

cards.title: Islamic golden age
cards.text: From roughly the 8th to 13th centuries, scholars in Baghdad, Cairo and Córdoba translated and extended Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy.

cards.title: Numbers we use
cards.text: The digits 0–9 came from India, reached Europe through the Arab world and are called Hindu-Arabic numerals. The word "algorithm" comes from al-Khwarizmi's name.

cards.title: Agriculture and irrigation
cards.text: Muslim farmers introduced or spread crops like oranges, lemons, rice, almonds and sugar cane in Iberia, along with irrigation systems such as the water wheel (nora).

cards.title: Arabic in Portuguese
cards.text: Portuguese has hundreds of words of Arabic origin, often starting with "al-": azeite, arroz, alface, almofada, açúcar, aldeia, armazém. "Oxalá" comes from "if God wills".

cards.title: Place names
cards.text: Many Portuguese places have Arabic names: the Algarve (al-gharb, "the west"), Alcácer, Alfama, Albufeira, Fátima (a Muslim name).

cards.title: The Reconquista
cards.text: Christian kingdoms in the north gradually pushed south over nearly 800 years. Portugal completed its reconquest with the Algarve in 1249; Spain with Granada in 1492.

cards.title: Silves and Mértola
cards.text: Silves was the capital of the Algarve under Muslim rule, and Mértola's church was once a mosque. Both still show their Islamic past in walls, streets and museums.

quiz.q: What did Muslims call Iberia?
The word "algorithm" comes from…
When did Portugal complete its reconquest?

lessons.title: The birth of Portugal
lessons.summary: From county to kingdom, and the battle that saved it.

cards.title: The County of Portucale
cards.text: Portugal began as a county of the kingdom of León, named after Portucale, today's Porto area. In 1096 it was given to Henry of Burgundy and his wife Teresa.

cards.title: São Mamede, 1128
cards.text: Young Afonso Henriques defeated his mother Teresa's forces at the Battle of São Mamede near Guimarães in 1128, taking control of the county. Guimarães is called "the cradle of Portugal".

cards.title: Recognition: 1143 and 1179
cards.text: At the Treaty of Zamora (1143), Alfonso VII of León recognised Afonso as king. The Pope formally confirmed it in 1179 with the bull Manifestis Probatum.

cards.title: Moving south
cards.text: Afonso and his successors took Santarém and Lisbon (1147), then the Alentejo and finally the Algarve (1249). Portugal's borders, set by the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297, are among Europe's oldest.

cards.title: King Dinis
cards.text: Dom Dinis (reigned 1279–1325) planted the pine forest of Leiria to protect farmland and supply timber, founded the university, made Portuguese the official language of documents and created the Order of Christ.

cards.title: The 1383–85 crisis
cards.text: When King Fernando died without a son, Castile claimed the throne. Many Portuguese backed João, Master of Avis. The crisis became a fight for independence.

cards.title: Aljubarrota, 1385
cards.text: On 14 August 1385, a smaller Portuguese army under Nuno Álvares Pereira and King João I, with English archers, defeated Castile at Aljubarrota using defensive tactics. Independence was secured.

cards.title: Batalha monastery
cards.text: João I built the Monastery of Santa Maria da Vitória at Batalha to give thanks for Aljubarrota. It's a UNESCO World Heritage site and a masterpiece of Gothic and Manueline art.

cards.title: The oldest alliance

events.l: João I marries Philippa of Lancaster

cards.text: The Treaty of Windsor (1386) between Portugal and England is the oldest diplomatic alliance in the world still in force. João I married Philippa of Lancaster, mother of Prince Henry the Navigator.

cards.title: The Avis dynasty
cards.text: The Avis kings launched the overseas expansion: Ceuta (1415), the Atlantic islands, the African coast and finally India. It was the start of Portugal's golden age.

quiz.q: Which city is called "the cradle of Portugal"?
quiz.explain: Afonso Henriques' base; São Mamede was nearby.

quiz.q: Who won the Battle of Aljubarrota in 1385?
What is the Treaty of Windsor (1386)?
options: The oldest diplomatic alliance still in force

lessons.title: The Renaissance
lessons.summary: Rebirth of art, science and ideas.

cards.title: A rebirth
cards.text: The Renaissance ("rebirth") began in Italy in the 1300s–1400s. Scholars rediscovered Greek and Roman texts, artists studied nature and the human body, and individuals were celebrated.

cards.title: Florence and patrons
cards.text: Florence led the way, funded by rich families like the Medici who sponsored artists, architects and scholars. Wealth from banking and trade paid for the art.

cards.title: Perspective
cards.text: Artists like Brunelleschi worked out linear perspective around 1420: parallel lines meet at a vanishing point, making flat paintings look three-dimensional.

cards.title: Leonardo da Vinci
cards.text: Painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, Leonardo (1452–1519) also filled notebooks with anatomy, flying machines, engineering and studies of water, a true "Renaissance man".

cards.title: Michelangelo
cards.text: Michelangelo (1475–1564) sculpted David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling, lying on scaffolding for four years. He also designed the dome of St Peter's in Rome.

cards.title: Humanism
cards.text: Humanists believed in studying classical texts, good writing and the potential of human beings. Erasmus of Rotterdam was its most famous northern European voice.

cards.title: Manueline style
cards.text: Portugal's own late-Gothic style, named after King Manuel I, decorates buildings with ropes, armillary spheres, sea creatures and coral, celebrating the voyages. The Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower are famous examples.

cards.title: Os Lusíadas
cards.text: Luís de Camões published Os Lusíadas in 1572, an epic poem about Vasco da Gama's voyage and Portuguese history, inspired by classical epics. Portugal's national day, 10 June, marks his death.

cards.title: Printing spreads the Renaissance
cards.text: Gutenberg's press (around 1450) let books and new ideas spread fast. Venice became a printing capital; the first book printed in Portugal appeared in 1487, in Hebrew, in Faro.

cards.title: Renaissance science
cards.text: Artists' careful observation fed into science: Vesalius' accurate anatomy (1543) and Copernicus' Sun-centred universe (1543) both appeared in the same year.

quiz.q: Which family famously sponsored Renaissance artists in Florence?
What is the Manueline style?
options: Portugal's ornate late-Gothic architecture with maritime motifs

quiz.q: Who wrote Os Lusíadas?

lessons.title: Reformation and Scientific Revolution
lessons.summary: New ideas about faith and nature.

cards.title: Luther's 95 theses

events.l: Church of England breaks with Rome

cards.text: In 1517, the monk Martin Luther challenged the Church's sale of indulgences (payments to reduce punishment for sins). His protest, spread by printing, split western Christianity.

cards.title: Protestant and Catholic
cards.text: Protestants stressed faith and the Bible read in people's own languages; the Catholic Church responded with the Counter-Reformation, reforming itself and founding orders like the Jesuits.

cards.title: Wars of religion
cards.text: Religious division fuelled wars across Europe for over a century, culminating in the devastating Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which killed millions in central Europe.

cards.title: The Inquisition in Portugal

events.l: Jews ordered to convert or leave

cards.text: The Portuguese Inquisition, established in 1536, persecuted New Christians (converted Jews), suspected heretics and others. Many Jewish families fled to the Netherlands, Ottoman lands and elsewhere. It was abolished in 1821.

cards.title: Copernicus
cards.text: In 1543 Copernicus argued that Earth and the planets orbit the Sun, not the other way round. It was a radical idea that took over a century to be widely accepted.

cards.title: Galileo's trial
cards.text: Galileo's telescope observations supported Copernicus. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition forced him to recant and kept him under house arrest. The Church formally acknowledged its error in 1992.

cards.title: The scientific method
cards.text: Thinkers like Francis Bacon and Descartes argued for learning through observation, experiment and reason rather than authority alone. This became the scientific method.

cards.title: Newton's synthesis
cards.text: Newton's Principia (1687) used a few laws to explain both falling objects and planetary orbits. It showed the universe follows mathematical rules, a turning point for science.

cards.title: Scientific societies
cards.text: Groups like the Royal Society in London (1660) and the French Academy of Sciences (1666) met to share experiments and published journals, the start of modern peer-reviewed science.

cards.title: Instruments
cards.text: Telescopes, microscopes, thermometers, barometers and pendulum clocks let scientists measure what they couldn't see before.

quiz.q: What did Luther protest against in 1517?
Copernicus proposed that…
What does the scientific method rely on?

lessons.title: The 1755 earthquake and the Enlightenment
lessons.summary: Lisbon destroyed, rebuilt and rethought.

cards.title: 1 November 1755
cards.text: On All Saints' Day morning, a huge earthquake struck off Portugal's coast. Churches were full and candles lit. Within minutes much of Lisbon collapsed.

cards.title: Earthquake, tsunami, fire
cards.text: The earthquake, estimated at magnitude 8.5–9, was followed by a tsunami up to several metres high and by fires that burned for days. Estimates of deaths in Lisbon range from about 30,000 to 50,000 or more.

cards.title: The Marquis of Pombal
cards.text: Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, later Marquis of Pombal, led the response: "bury the dead and feed the living". He organised relief, controlled prices and planned the rebuilding.

cards.title: The new Baixa
cards.text: The Baixa was rebuilt on a grid of wide straight streets with uniform buildings, using standardised parts and the earthquake-resistant gaiola pombalina.

cards.title: The birth of seismology
cards.text: Pombal sent a questionnaire to every parish: when did it start, how long did it last, what damage occurred? It was one of the first systematic scientific studies of an earthquake.

cards.title: Shaking European thought
cards.text: The disaster shocked Europe's thinkers. Voltaire questioned why a good God would allow it, in his "Poem on the Lisbon Disaster" and in Candide. Rousseau answered that city crowding made it worse.

cards.title: The Enlightenment
cards.text: The 18th-century Enlightenment championed reason, science, religious tolerance and individual rights. Thinkers like Locke, Montesquieu, Voltaire and Kant inspired revolutions.

cards.title: Pombal's reforms
cards.text: Pombal modernised education and trade, expelled the Jesuits (1759), created the Douro wine demarcation (1756), one of the world's first, and reduced discrimination against New Christians.

cards.title: The Encyclopédie
cards.text: Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie (1751–1772) gathered knowledge on everything from trades to philosophy, spreading Enlightenment ideas across Europe.

cards.title: Lessons for today
cards.text: Lisbon still sits near active faults. Modern building codes, tsunami warnings and earthquake drills draw on lessons from 1755.

quiz.q: When did the great Lisbon earthquake strike?
Who led the rebuilding of Lisbon?
Which Enlightenment writer questioned divine goodness after the disaster?
quiz.explain: In his poem and in Candide.

lessons.title: The age of revolutions
lessons.summary: America, France, Napoleon and Portugal.

cards.title: The American Revolution
cards.text: Thirteen British colonies rebelled over taxation without representation. The Declaration of Independence (1776) proclaimed that all men are created equal, though slavery continued.

cards.title: The French Revolution
cards.text: In 1789, with France bankrupt and bread expensive, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly and Parisians stormed the Bastille. Feudal privileges were abolished.

cards.title: Liberty, equality, fraternity
cards.text: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) proclaimed equality before the law, freedom of speech and the sovereignty of the nation, ideas that spread worldwide.

cards.title: The Terror
cards.text: In 1793–94, the revolutionary government executed thousands of suspected enemies by guillotine, including many revolutionaries themselves, until Robespierre himself was executed.

cards.title: Napoleon
cards.text: Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in 1799, crowned himself emperor in 1804 and conquered much of Europe. His Napoleonic Code influenced law across Europe, including Portugal.

cards.title: The French invasions of Portugal
cards.text: Because Portugal kept trading with Britain, Napoleon invaded three times from 1807. With British help under Wellington, the Portuguese resisted, including at the Lines of Torres Vedras.

cards.title: The court flees to Brazil
cards.text: In 1807, as the French approached, the royal family and thousands of courtiers sailed to Brazil. Rio de Janeiro became the capital of the Portuguese empire, the only time a European capital moved to a colony.

cards.title: Brazil's independence
cards.text: After the king returned to Portugal, his son Pedro stayed in Brazil and declared independence on 7 September 1822, becoming Emperor Pedro I.

cards.title: The Liberal Revolution
cards.text: The 1820 revolution in Porto demanded a constitution. A civil war (1828–1834) between liberals under Pedro and absolutists under his brother Miguel ended with the liberals' victory.

cards.title: Revolutions in Latin America
cards.text: Inspired by the US and France, and helped by Spain's weakness under Napoleon, most of Spanish America won independence between 1810 and 1825, led by figures like Simón Bolívar.

quiz.q: Why did Napoleon invade Portugal?
options: Portugal kept trading with Britain against his blockade

quiz.q: Where did the Portuguese court move in 1807?
When did Brazil declare independence?

lessons.title: The 19th century
lessons.summary: Industry, railways, empires and new ideas.

cards.title: Railways
cards.text: The first public steam railway opened in England in 1825. Railways shrank journeys from days to hours and opened markets. Portugal's first line, Lisbon to Carregado, opened in 1856.

cards.title: Steamships and telegraph

viz.unit: days for a London–New York message

cards.text: Steamships made ocean travel reliable, and the telegraph carried messages instantly. The first lasting transatlantic cable (1866) cut message times from weeks to minutes.

cards.title: Cities and factories
cards.text: Millions moved from farms to industrial cities. Conditions were harsh: long hours, child labour, crowded housing and polluted air. Reforms, unions and new laws slowly improved them.

cards.title: New ideologies
cards.text: The 19th century produced liberalism, nationalism, socialism and Marxism, ideas about the state, nations and workers that shaped the next century.

cards.title: Abolition of slavery
cards.text: Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1833. Portugal abolished slavery in stages, completing it in 1869–1878; Brazil was the last in the Americas, in 1888.

cards.title: The Scramble for Africa
cards.text: At the Berlin Conference (1884–85), European powers set rules for dividing Africa. By 1914, almost the whole continent was under European control.

cards.title: The Pink Map and the Ultimatum
cards.text: Portugal hoped to link Angola and Mozambique (the "Pink Map"). Britain, wanting a Cape-to-Cairo route, issued the 1890 Ultimatum, forcing Portugal to back down, a national humiliation that fuelled republicanism.

cards.title: Science and medicine
cards.text: Darwin's theory of evolution (1859), Pasteur's germ theory, vaccines, anaesthesia and antiseptic surgery transformed biology and medicine.

cards.title: Unification of Italy and Germany
cards.text: Italy unified between 1859 and 1871 and Germany in 1871 under Prussia, changing Europe's balance of power and setting the stage for rivalries before 1914.

cards.title: Electricity and the telephone
cards.text: In the last decades of the century came the telephone (1876), the light bulb (1879), electric power stations, cars (1886) and radio, the foundations of the 20th century.

quiz.q: When did Portugal's first railway open?
What was the 1890 British Ultimatum about?
options: Portugal's plan to link Angola and Mozambique

quiz.q: Which country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery?

lessons.title: World War I
lessons.summary: The Great War, 1914–1918.

cards.title: The spark
cards.text: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary was assassinated in Sarajevo. Alliances, militarism and rivalry turned a regional crisis into a world war within weeks.

cards.title: Two alliances
cards.text: The Allies (France, Britain, Russia, later Italy, the USA and others including Portugal) fought the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Bulgaria).

cards.title: Trench warfare
cards.text: On the Western Front, armies dug trenches from the Channel to Switzerland. Machine guns and artillery made attacks deadly; battles like the Somme cost hundreds of thousands of lives for a few kilometres.

cards.title: New weapons
cards.text: WWI introduced poison gas, tanks, warplanes, submarines and industrial-scale artillery. War had become mechanised.

cards.title: Portugal at war
cards.text: Portugal fought in Africa to defend Angola and Mozambique, and from 1917 sent the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps to Flanders. At La Lys on 9 April 1918, Portuguese forces suffered heavy losses.

cards.title: The home front
cards.text: Whole economies served the war. Women took over factory and farm work, food was rationed and governments controlled production and news.

cards.title: The USA joins
cards.text: German submarine attacks and the Zimmermann telegram drew the USA into the war in 1917. Fresh American troops helped tip the balance in 1918. Russia left the war after its revolution.

cards.title: The human cost
cards.text: Around 9–10 million soldiers and millions of civilians died. Then the 1918 flu pandemic killed tens of millions more worldwide.

cards.title: The Treaty of Versailles
cards.text: The 1919 peace treaty blamed Germany, imposed heavy reparations and took territory. Empires collapsed: Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and the Russian Empire. New nations appeared.

cards.title: Seeds of the next war
cards.text: Resentment in Germany, economic crisis and unresolved disputes helped extremists rise, leading to another world war only 20 years later.

quiz.q: What event triggered WWI?
options: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand

quiz.q: Where did Portuguese troops suffer heavy losses on 9 April 1918?
When did the armistice end the fighting?

lessons.title: Between the wars
lessons.summary: Republics, the Depression and dictatorships.

cards.title: The roaring twenties
cards.text: After the war, the 1920s brought jazz, cinema, radio, cars and booming stock markets in the USA, along with new freedoms for women, including the vote in many countries.

cards.title: The 1929 crash
cards.text: In October 1929 the New York stock market collapsed. Banks failed, trade shrank and unemployment soared worldwide: the Great Depression.

cards.title: The Soviet Union
cards.text: After the 1917 revolution, the Bolsheviks created the Soviet Union. Under Stalin, forced collectivisation and purges killed millions, including in the Ukrainian famine (Holodomor) of 1932–33.

cards.title: Fascism in Italy
cards.text: Mussolini took power in 1922 and built a one-party state with censorship, a personality cult and aggressive nationalism: fascism.

cards.title: Hitler's rise
cards.text: In Germany, the Depression helped the Nazi party grow. Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and quickly destroyed democracy, persecuted Jews and opponents, and rearmed.

cards.title: The First Portuguese Republic
cards.text: The monarchy fell on 5 October 1910. The First Republic separated church and state and expanded education, but was unstable: 45 governments in 16 years.

cards.title: The Estado Novo begins
cards.text: After a military coup in 1926, finance minister António de Oliveira Salazar became prime minister in 1932 and created the Estado Novo, an authoritarian, corporatist regime with censorship and a political police (PVDE, later PIDE).

cards.title: The Spanish Civil War
cards.text: From 1936 to 1939, Spain's republic fought Franco's nationalists, who were helped by Germany and Italy. Franco won and ruled Spain until 1975. Portugal's regime supported Franco.

cards.title: The New Deal
cards.text: In the USA, Roosevelt's New Deal created public works, social security and bank regulation to fight the Depression, expanding the role of government.

cards.title: Appeasement
cards.text: Britain and France tried to avoid war by giving in to Hitler's demands, accepting Austria's annexation and, at Munich in 1938, part of Czechoslovakia. It failed.

quiz.q: When was the Portuguese republic proclaimed?
What began in October 1929?
options: The Great Depression, with the Wall Street crash

quiz.q: Who created Portugal's Estado Novo?

lessons.title: World War II
lessons.summary: 1939–1945, the deadliest conflict in history.

cards.title: The war begins

events.l: Denmark, Norway, Low Countries, France fall

cards.text: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war. By mid-1940, Germany had conquered much of western Europe, including France.

cards.title: A world war
cards.text: In 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union, and Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, bringing the USA into the war. Fighting spread across Europe, Africa, Asia and the oceans.

cards.title: The Holocaust
cards.text: Nazi Germany systematically murdered about six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners, political opponents and others, in ghettos, mass shootings and death camps like Auschwitz.

cards.title: Aristides de Sousa Mendes

steps: Sousa Mendes issues thousands of visas

cards.text: In June 1940, Portugal's consul in Bordeaux, Aristides de Sousa Mendes, defied Salazar's orders and issued thousands of visas to refugees, many of them Jews. He was punished and died poor; he's now honoured as Righteous Among the Nations.

cards.title: Neutral Portugal

items: Neutral but pro-Allied in the end

cards.text: Portugal stayed officially neutral, selling tungsten (volfrâmio) to both sides. Lisbon became a hub of spies and a gateway for refugees escaping to the Americas. In 1943 it let the Allies use bases in the Azores.

cards.title: D-Day
cards.text: On 6 June 1944, Allied forces landed in Normandy in the largest seaborne invasion in history, opening a western front as the Soviets advanced from the east.

cards.title: The end in Europe
cards.text: Soviet troops took Berlin; Hitler killed himself; Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945 (VE Day).

cards.title: Atomic bombs
cards.text: The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August), killing well over 100,000 people. Japan surrendered on 15 August, formally on 2 September.

cards.title: The cost
cards.text: World War II killed an estimated 70–85 million people, most of them civilians. The Soviet Union and China suffered the largest losses.

cards.title: After the war
cards.text: The United Nations was founded in 1945, war criminals were tried at Nuremberg, and Europe was divided between western democracies and Soviet-controlled states.

quiz.q: Which Portuguese consul saved thousands of refugees in 1940?
What happened on 6 June 1944?
What did Portugal sell to both sides during WWII?
quiz.explain: A vital metal for armour and tools.

lessons.title: The Cold War
lessons.summary: Superpowers, nuclear fear and a divided world, 1947–1991.

cards.title: Two superpowers
cards.text: After 1945, the USA and the Soviet Union became rival superpowers with opposing systems: capitalist democracy versus communist one-party rule. They never fought each other directly.

cards.title: The Iron Curtain
cards.text: Europe was split. Churchill spoke of an "iron curtain" in 1946. Germany was divided, and in 1961 East Germany built the Berlin Wall to stop people fleeing west.

cards.title: The nuclear arms race
cards.text: Both sides built tens of thousands of nuclear weapons. The doctrine of "mutually assured destruction" meant any nuclear war would destroy both.

cards.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
cards.text: In October 1962, the USA discovered Soviet missiles in Cuba. For 13 days the world stood close to nuclear war, until the USSR agreed to withdraw them and the USA quietly removed missiles from Turkey.

cards.title: Proxy wars
cards.text: The superpowers fought indirectly by backing opposite sides in other conflicts: Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and wars in Africa, including Angola after 1975.

cards.title: The space race
cards.text: The USSR launched Sputnik (1957) and Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space (1961). The USA landed Apollo 11 astronauts on the Moon on 20 July 1969.

cards.title: Portugal in NATO
cards.text: Despite being a dictatorship, Portugal was a founding member of NATO in 1949, largely because of the strategic Azores base. Its colonial wars from 1961 strained relations with allies.

cards.title: Détente and reform
cards.text: In the 1970s tensions eased with arms control treaties. In the 1980s Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms, glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), loosened Soviet control.

cards.title: The Wall falls
cards.text: On 9 November 1989 the Berlin Wall opened. Communist governments across eastern Europe collapsed within months, Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

cards.title: Legacy
cards.text: The Cold War shaped borders, alliances, technologies like the internet and GPS (both born from military research), and conflicts that still echo today.

quiz.q: When did the Berlin Wall fall?
Who was the first human in space?
Why was dictatorship-era Portugal a NATO founding member?
options: The Azores base was strategically important

lessons.title: Portugal in the 20th century
lessons.summary: Dictatorship, colonial wars, revolution and Europe.

cards.title: Life under the Estado Novo
cards.text: Salazar's regime rested on "God, Fatherland, Family". It censored the press, banned parties and strikes, used the political police PIDE, and kept Portugal poor and largely rural, with high emigration.

cards.title: Emigration
cards.text: From the 1950s to the 1970s, well over a million Portuguese emigrated, many illegally ("a salto") to France, Germany and Luxembourg, escaping poverty and military service.

cards.title: The colonial wars
cards.text: From 1961 Portugal fought independence movements in Angola, Guinea-Bissau and Mozambique. Over 13 years, about 800,000 Portuguese men served; around 9,000 died, along with many more Africans.

cards.title: Humberto Delgado

events.l: murdered by the PIDE in Spain

cards.text: In the 1958 presidential election, General Humberto Delgado challenged the regime. Asked what he'd do with Salazar, he said: "Obviamente, demito-o!" He lost a fraudulent vote and was murdered by the PIDE in 1965.

cards.title: Salazar to Caetano
cards.text: Salazar was incapacitated in 1968 after a fall and replaced by Marcelo Caetano, who promised reforms but kept the colonial wars and the regime's core.

cards.title: 25 de Abril, 1974

events.l: 20: "Grândola, Vila Morena" on the radio signals go
Caetano surrenders at Largo do Carmo

cards.text: On 25 April 1974, young officers of the Armed Forces Movement (MFA) overthrew the regime almost without bloodshed. Crowds filled the streets and put carnations in soldiers' rifles: the Carnation Revolution.

cards.title: Decolonisation

events.l: Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, Angola

cards.text: After the revolution, Portugal recognised the independence of Guinea-Bissau (1974), Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Angola (1975). Around half a million "retornados" came to Portugal.

cards.title: Building democracy
cards.text: After a turbulent period (PREC), the 1976 constitution established a democratic republic. Free elections, a free press and local democracy took root.

cards.title: Joining Europe
cards.text: Portugal joined the European Economic Community on 1 January 1986 together with Spain. EU funds helped build roads, schools and hospitals; Portugal adopted the euro in 1999 (coins and notes in 2002).

cards.title: Expo '98 and modern Portugal
cards.text: Expo '98 in Lisbon transformed the eastern waterfront and showcased a modern country. Since then Portugal has faced crises (2011 bailout) and become a major tourism and tech destination.

quiz.q: What signalled the start of the 25 April 1974 revolution on the radio?
When did Portugal join the European Economic Community?
Which general famously said "Obviamente, demito-o!"?

lessons.title: The world since 1945
lessons.summary: Decolonisation, globalisation and new challenges.

cards.title: The end of empires
cards.text: Between 1945 and 1975, most colonies in Asia and Africa became independent: India and Pakistan (1947), Indonesia, Ghana (1957), dozens of African nations around 1960, and the Portuguese colonies in 1974–75.

cards.title: Civil rights
cards.text: Movements fought discrimination: the US civil rights movement led by Martin Luther King Jr., the end of apartheid in South Africa with Nelson Mandela's election in 1994, and women's rights movements worldwide.

cards.title: European integration
cards.text: From the 1951 coal and steel community, European cooperation grew into the EU: a single market, free movement, and for many members, the euro.

cards.title: China's rise
cards.text: After Mao's era, Deng Xiaoping's reforms from 1978 opened China's economy. Hundreds of millions escaped poverty, and China became the world's manufacturing centre.

cards.title: Globalisation
cards.text: Container shipping, cheaper flights, trade agreements and the internet tied economies together. Goods are made from parts produced in many countries.

cards.title: Extreme poverty falls
cards.text: The share of people in extreme poverty fell from roughly half of humanity in 1950 to under 10% before the pandemic, one of history's great achievements, though progress is uneven.

cards.title: 11 September 2001
cards.text: Terrorist attacks on New York and Washington killed nearly 3,000 people and led to wars in Afghanistan and Iraq and a global focus on terrorism.

cards.title: Financial crisis
cards.text: The 2008 crash, starting with US housing loans, triggered a global recession and, in Europe, a debt crisis that led to bailouts of Greece, Ireland and Portugal.

cards.title: Pandemic
cards.text: COVID-19 spread worldwide from early 2020, causing millions of deaths, lockdowns and the fastest vaccine development in history.

cards.title: Climate change
cards.text: Since the 1980s scientists have warned of global warming from greenhouse gases. The 2015 Paris Agreement set the goal of limiting warming to well below 2 °C.

quiz.q: When was Nelson Mandela elected president of South Africa?
What happened to extreme poverty between 1950 and 2019?
options: It fell from about half of humanity to under 10%

quiz.q: What goal did the 2015 Paris Agreement set?

lessons.title: The digital revolution
lessons.summary: From room-sized computers to smartphones and AI.

cards.title: Early computers
cards.text: Wartime code-breaking and calculations drove early electronic computers. ENIAC (1945) filled a room, weighed 27 tonnes and used about 18,000 vacuum tubes.

cards.title: The transistor and the chip
cards.text: The transistor (1947) and the integrated circuit (1958) made computers smaller, cheaper and more reliable. Intel's 4004 (1971) put a whole processor on one chip.

cards.title: Personal computers
cards.text: In the late 1970s and 1980s, computers entered homes and offices: the Apple II (1977), IBM PC (1981), Macintosh (1984) and Microsoft Windows. In Portugal the ZX Spectrum (Timex) was hugely popular.

cards.title: The internet
cards.text: ARPANET connected US research computers in 1969. TCP/IP (1983) let networks join into one internet. Portugal connected to the internet in the early 1990s through its universities.

cards.title: The World Wide Web
cards.text: At CERN in 1989–91, Tim Berners-Lee invented the web: web pages, links and browsers on top of the internet. He gave it away for free.

cards.title: Search and social media
cards.text: Google (1998) organised the web; Facebook (2004), YouTube (2005) and Twitter (2006) made everyone a publisher, changing news, politics and friendship.

cards.title: Mobile phones
cards.text: Mobile phones spread fast in the 1990s; Portugal had one of Europe's highest adoption rates. The iPhone (2007) and Android turned phones into pocket computers.

cards.title: Multibanco
cards.text: Portugal's Multibanco network, launched in 1985, was one of the world's most advanced ATM systems, letting people pay bills, top up phones and buy tickets long before this was common elsewhere.

cards.title: Cloud and data
cards.text: Since the 2000s, computing moved into huge data centres. Companies rent servers on demand (AWS 2006, Azure 2010), and data became one of the most valuable resources.

cards.title: The AI era
cards.text: Deep learning (2012), the Transformer (2017) and ChatGPT (2022) opened a new chapter: computers that understand and generate language, images and code.

quiz.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
When was Portugal's Multibanco network launched?
quiz.explain: One of the world's most advanced ATM systems.

quiz.q: What was ARPANET?
options: An early US research network, forerunner of the internet
